problem: Existing navigation simulators (Habitat, AI2-THOR) rely on reconstructed or synthetic meshes with unrealistic rendering, and hand-built game-engine scenes do not scale to multi-room or whole-floor environments. Prior large-scale 3DGS works also lack collision modeling for navigation.
motivation: Navigation needs high-fidelity, large-scale scenes spanning rooms or floors, and sim-to-real transfer depends on rendering realism. 3DGS reconstructs real environments easily and renders photorealistically, but it needs a way to derive navigable areas and a usable API to become a simulator.
key_idea: Build a navigation simulator on hierarchical 3D Gaussian Splatting for large-scale photorealistic rendering, with an analytic multi-height Gaussian slicing method that turns the Gaussians into a 2D occupancy map for collision checking.
insight: Rendering fidelity matters for sim-to-real: a simulator built on plain 3DGS (PSNR 23.221 vs 25.396) reaches a similar sim SR level but a much lower real SR (13.7 vs 69.2 average on annotated targets). Pretraining (VQA/video-language data) speeds up learning and gives >90% SR after two DAgger rounds, whereas training from scratch plateaus lower (shown in a figure only). All experiments use one 700 m² scene, so the evidence is narrow.
method: Hierarchical 3DGS scenes: H3DGS tree with LOD rendering; the input images are split into chunks optimized independently, then merged into a global hierarchy using multiple GPUs in parallel.

GS-Slice collision: horizontal planes at fixed height intervals (e.g. 10 cm) within the robot's height range; each 3D Gaussian is analytically sliced into a 2D Gaussian (closed-form center and covariance, with a decay term in z), and the slices are combined into a 2D occupancy map, with collision volume error under 5 cm.
NavGSim-API: Python library for scene reconstruction from posed RGB, robot configuration, multi-GPU policy training and evaluation, plus an interactive annotation/visualization interface.

VLA-NavGSim: Uni-NaVid extension (EVA-CLIP frozen, online token merging, Vicuna-7B fully fine-tuned) that runs a single LLM step and feeds the final hidden state to an MLP head predicting a continuous (x,y,θ) trajectory.

Data collection: 9 annotated landmarks, 200 shortest-path expert trajectories each, plus two DAgger rounds of 150 trajectories per landmark; DAgger rollouts end on 8 consecutive collisions, step budget, or success; co-trained with ScanQA/Panda/LLaMA-style VQA data.
Stop via velocity modulation: speed decays within 2 m of the target; the agent is halted when velocity drops to 0.1 m/s.

setting.backbone: Uni-NaVid-based VLA: EVA-CLIP (frozen) + Vicuna-7B (fully fine-tuned) + MLP trajectory head
setting.training_data: 4,500 simulated navigation trajectories in one 700 m² office scene (200 expert + 2 DAgger rounds x 150 per each of 9 landmarks) plus public VQA data (ScanQA etc.); 16 H800 GPUs for 20 h
setting.observation: egocentric monocular RGB frame sequence plus language instruction
setting.action_space: continuous predicted trajectory (x, y, θ) in the agent frame; velocity-modulated stopping
setting.privileged: none (expert shortest-path planner used only for training supervision)

numbers_note: Custom single-scene benchmark, no standard benchmark. Pretraining ablation only in a figure (>90% SR after two DAgger rounds). Rendering quality table: H3DGS PSNR 25.396, LPIPS 0.274, SSIM 0.866; 3DGS 23.221, 0.426, 0.789.
results: The VLA trained in NavGSim reaches 98.3% sim SR (0.91 m DTG) on annotated targets and 80.8% on novel targets, and 69.2% real-robot SR without real data. The plain-3DGS simulator gives 80.8% sim SR but only 13.7% real SR, so H3DGS rendering matters for sim-to-real.
limitations: Hierarchical GS preprocessing is slow for large scenes, limiting fast iteration on new environments.
No dynamic scene editing (adding or removing objects after reconstruction).
Evaluation covers a single 700 m² office scene with no comparison to mesh-based simulators or standard benchmarks; the real-world trial count is small.
